trails.trailTip: The fire lookout tower at the top is staffed only seasonally and isn't always open to visitors — check with the visitor center for current tower hours before you go.
trails.didYouKnow: At about 5,013 feet, Rankin Ridge is the highest point in Wind Cave National Park, with views stretching across the prairie to the Black Hills.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, overnight backcountry camping anywhere off the Centennial Trail within Wind Cave requires a free permit obtained in person at the visitor center — no permit is needed for a day hike on this segment.
trails.didYouKnow: The Centennial Trail runs 111 miles across the Black Hills, and this segment through Wind Cave is one of the few parts that crosses open mixed-grass prairie rather than forest.

trails.trailTip: This easy loop starts right at the Elk Mountain Campground, making it a convenient stretch-your-legs option for campers before or after a cave tour.
trails.didYouKnow: Despite the name, the trail passes through ponderosa pine forest more often frequented by white-tailed deer than elk, which favor the open prairie.

trails.trailTip: This trail connects to the Centennial Trail, so pick up a park map before heading out to avoid an unplanned longer loop.
trails.didYouKnow: The open prairie along this trail is part of one of the largest remaining mixed-grass prairie ecosystems in the country.

trails.trailTip: This dry canyon is a good spot to look and listen for cliff-nesting birds — bring binoculars and view any nest sites from the canyon floor rather than climbing toward the walls.
trails.didYouKnow: The canyon has no flowing water most of the year, carved instead by rare but intense flash floods over thousands of years.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, a free backcountry camping permit — available at the visitor center — is required for any overnight stay along this trail, even though no permit is needed for a day hike.
trails.didYouKnow: At 7.1 miles, this is the longest surface trail in the park, crossing both open prairie and forested draws along Highland Creek.

trails.trailTip: There's little shade on this exposed ridge climb, so carry extra water and start early on warm days.
trails.didYouKnow: The ridge offers one of the widest views in the park of the transition zone where prairie grasslands meet Black Hills forest.

trails.trailTip: This trail sees far fewer visitors than those near the visitor center — let someone know your plan, since the route is less clearly marked than the park's more popular trails.
trails.didYouKnow: The canyon's limestone walls are part of the same cave-forming rock layer that riddles the underground passages of Wind Cave itself.

animals.whereToLook: Open prairie along US Highway 385 and the park's scenic drives
animals.viewingTip: View bison from your vehicle or from at least 100 yards away on foot — they can run over 30 mph and become especially unpredictable during the summer rut, so never approach for a photo no matter how calm a herd looks.
animals.didYouKnow: Wind Cave's bison herd descends from animals reintroduced in 1913, making it one of the oldest continuously managed public bison herds in the country.

animals.whereToLook: Prairie dog towns visible from park roads, especially near the visitor center
animals.viewingTip: Watch from the roadside or a pullout rather than walking into a town — burrows can twist an ankle, and prairie dogs will dive underground the moment you get too close, cutting off their natural behavior.
animals.didYouKnow: Prairie dog towns support an entire ecosystem, providing burrows for burrowing owls and prey for badgers, coyotes, and black-footed ferrets.

animals.whereToLook: Ponderosa pine forest edges bordering the prairie
animals.viewingTip: During the fall rut, bull elk can be aggressive and unpredictable — stay at least 100 yards away and never position yourself between a bull and its herd, viewing the bugling display through binoculars instead.
animals.didYouKnow: A bull elk's bugle can carry over a mile across open prairie and forest, a key part of the fall rutting display.

animals.whereToLook: Open grassland along the park's main roads
animals.viewingTip: Pull off the road fully before stopping to watch a herd, and use binoculars rather than approaching on foot — pronghorn rely on keen eyesight and will bolt at the first sign of an approaching person.
animals.didYouKnow: Pronghorn evolved their speed to outrun a now-extinct American cheetah, making them far faster than any predator they face today.

animals.whereToLook: Roosts deep within Wind Cave's passages, not typically visible on standard tours
animals.viewingTip: Never touch cave walls or formations on a tour, and follow all ranger instructions about decontaminating gear — roosting bat colonies are extremely sensitive to disturbance, and human-introduced fungus has devastated bat populations elsewhere.
animals.didYouKnow: Townsend's big-eared bats can wrap their large ears around their bodies while roosting, possibly to conserve heat during hibernation.

animals.viewingTip: Never feed a coyote — a fed coyote quickly loses its wariness of people, which puts both the animal and future visitors at risk; watch from a distance with binoculars instead.
animals.didYouKnow: Coyotes here hunt prairie dogs as a major food source, helping keep prairie dog town populations in balance.

animals.whereToLook: Soaring over prairie and ridge thermals, especially near Rankin Ridge
animals.viewingTip: Watch soaring eagles with binoculars from a distance rather than approaching a cliffside nest site if you spot one — golden eagles will abandon a nest if repeatedly disturbed during nesting season.
animals.didYouKnow: Golden eagles can spot a rabbit from nearly two miles away thanks to eyesight several times sharper than a human's.

animals.whereToLook: Near cave entrances and twilight zones on any cave tour
animals.viewingTip: Look but don't touch — cave crickets are harmless and a normal part of the cave ecosystem, and handling any cave-dwelling species risks introducing contaminants harmful to more sensitive species like bats.
animals.didYouKnow: Cave crickets have no wings and use extremely long antennae, sometimes longer than their bodies, to feel their way through total darkness.
